extracted.intended_audience: employers, industry stakeholders, occupational safety professionals, and public commenters on OSHA's Heat Injury and Illness Prevention proposed standard
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the technological-feasibility criteria, measurement requirements, and engineering-control expectations in OSHA's proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard (NPRM). Relevant to assessing what employers must measure, what controls are required when triggers are exceeded, and practical/technical limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technological feasibility (case-law definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A standard is technologically feasible if the protective measures it requires already exist, can be brought into existence with available technology, or can be created with technology that can reasonably be expected to be developed (American Textile Mfrs. Inst. v. Donovan; United Steelworkers v. Marshall; Am. Iron & Steel Inst. v. OSHA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must prove by substantial evidence that the standard is technologically and economically feasible. The agency reviewed requirements of the proposed Heat Injury and Illness Prevention standard and preliminarily determined compliance is technologically feasible. Use of precedent cases frames the feasibility inquiry as existence/availability/anticipated development of the required protective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Group establishments by work setting & heat source for feasibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For analyzing feasibility, group establishments by indoor work settings (heat-generating processes versus ambient heat) and outdoor work settings (ambient heat at fixed locations and transient/mobile sites) based on similarity of worker exposure sources (equipment/process-generated heat vs ambient heat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA used groups to assess which requirements imply engineering controls or address facility/equipment aspects versus programs/processes. Table IX-1 provides example facility types/occupations under each grouping to guide applicability and feasibility judgments across industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental monitoring requirement (HI, WBGT, AT)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule includes requirements for employers to monitor environmental conditions to determine whether certain controls need to be implemented when exposures meet or exceed specified triggers expressed in terms of heat index (HI), wet bulb globe temperature (WBGT), or ambient temperature (AT).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA must determine whether available methods exist for measuring HI, WBGT, and AT; the document evaluates available instruments and methods and preliminarily concludes that all three metrics can be monitored via instruments currently on the market.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat Index (HI) measurement feasibility and acceptable methods
rubrics_metrics.description: HI combines ambient temperature and either dew point or relative humidity to reflect the temperature the body 'feels.' Methods to determine HI include direct-read monitoring devices (heat-stress or heat-index monitors), psychrometers and thermometers with charts/calculators, and NOAA/NWS charts/calculators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most accurate for worksites is on-site direct-reading devices (handheld heat-stress monitors). Psychrometers and thermometers (digital/analog) with charts or online calculators are acceptable. For outdoor sites, employers may use local forecast weather data to estimate HI (including OSHA-NIOSH Heat Safety Tool which pulls hourly NWS forecasts), but OSHA does not propose permitting forecast data for indoor HI determinations. OSHA preliminarily concludes exposure assessments using HI are technologically feasible for most operations most of the time and seeks comments on measuring HI in different environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: WBGT measurement feasibility and instrument considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: WBGT is a measure that incorporates globe temperature, wet bulb temperature, and dry bulb temperature (accounts for AT, RH, wind speed, and solar radiation). WBGTs are measured with specialized equipment (standard instrument includes a 0.15 m black globe and a wetted thermometer), and various commercial WBGT monitors exist (e.g., QUESTemp, Kestrel handhelds).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although accurate WBGT instruments are commercially available, some lower-cost/non-standard monitors may not align with traditional WBGT measurements. Key technical considerations include inconsistent equilibration times, insufficient calibration procedures, and non-standard globe/wet bulb thermometers; smaller globes change sensitivity to short-term variations. Using WBGT on-site will require training to properly operate, and the extent of training depends on monitor type. OSHA seeks comments on practicality and challenges of WBGT measurement in different situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambient Temperature (AT) measurement feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: AT is air temperature measured using thermometers (liquid-in-glass, electrical thermocouples, resistance thermometers/thermistors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thermometer types are widely commercially available in many designs. States with permanent outdoor occupational heat standards (California, Washington) use fixed AT thresholds, supporting the metric's feasibility. OSHA preliminarily determines assessing AT in the workplace is technologically feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable monitoring options & indoor/outdoor distinctions
rubrics_metrics.description: Several instruments and methods can determine HI and WBGT (commercial devices like Kestrel and QUESTemp, mobile apps supported by NWS/NIOSH). For outdoor sites, employers may track local heat index forecasts in lieu of on-site measurement; for indoor sites, on-site measurements are required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA preliminarily concludes the technology necessary to comply with monitoring requirements exists and is commercially available; it requests additional comment on environments where particular metrics might not be practical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engineering controls obligation (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Engineering controls are measures that reduce, isolate, or remove a hazard from the workplace and do not rely on employee behavior. When exposures exceed specified triggers, employers must implement feasible controls to reduce employee exposures to heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineering controls are often most effective and can be cost-effective. Employers may choose any combination of effective engineering controls; the proposed standard differentiates requirements based on location (indoor vs outdoor) and whether exposures are from ambient heat or heat-generating processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Required controls & break area provisions (indoor vs outdoor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the proposed standard, when exposures exceed triggers, employers must implement feasible controls. For indoor work sites employers are required to provide a break area and ensure work areas exceeding the trigger are equipped with air-conditioning, fans and ventilation, or (for radiant heat) other controls to reduce heat exposure. For outdoor sites, employers are required to provide a break area with either shade or air-conditioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule does not prescribe a single mandatory engineering control for all indoor workplaces; employers are allowed to choose effective combinations. OSHA requests comments and data on feasibility in various contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controls specifically for heat-generating processes (indoor)
rubrics_metrics.description: For employees exposed to radiant heat from equipment/processes (e.g., ovens, foundries, steam pipes), the proposed rule requires employers to cool each indoor work area using either controls that increase evaporative heat loss from the worker (air-conditioning or fans) or controls that remove the worker's exposure to radiant heat in the workspace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engineering approaches include reducing radiant heat in workspace (lower process temperature, relocate/isolate source, insulate/cool source, change emissivity) or shielding workers (line-of-sight barriers, reflective shielding). Radiant reflective shielding can reduce radiant heat load by ~80–85%. Employers must consider process flow and feasibility; OSHA requests comments on outdoor applicability and other isolation methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific engineering-control techniques for heat-generating processes (Table IX-2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of control methods: local exhaust ventilation (LEV) at heat-generating sources; installation of waste heat recovery technology (regenerative/recuperative burners, tube heat exchangers); isolating the source (process enclosures, containment); shielding or barriers (reflective shields, absorbent shields like water-cooled jackets); thermal insulation on hot surfaces; increasing distance between workers and heat source.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table IX-2 gives installation examples and use-cases (e.g., LEV at laundry exhausts, reflective shields of stainless steel/aluminum, insulation to reduce emissivity). Employers can select among these depending on process constraints and compatibility with production requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process modification and automation as feasible controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Modifying the process or operation to reduce radiant heat—e.g., using materials with lower melting points, chemicals with faster curing, limiting task duration, or automating certain tasks (such as sample collection)—is considered a control option.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lowering process temperatures may conflict with manufacturing requirements; OSHA recognizes tradeoffs but identifies process/material changes and automation as potential feasible measures. OSHA solicits information on other practical process modifications employers have used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-conditioning as a control: efficacy and practicability limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Air-conditioning is highly effective at reducing heat strain and is widely available, but may not be practical in all occupational settings (e.g., outdoors, large factories, some industrial plants, and food-production areas with safety constraints).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is not requiring facility-wide air-conditioning. Evidence and studies show AC can maintain target indoor temperatures and can be used for break areas; however, feasibility depends on facility design, scale, insulation, and economic considerations. OSHA requests information on current AC use across covered industries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humidity control requirement when AC not provided
rubrics_metrics.description: For indoor work sites, employers who do not provide air-conditioned break areas or workspaces must implement humidity control (when appropriate) in conjunction with some form of air movement in those spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stand-alone dehumidifiers and HVAC-based dehumidification are commercially available; exhaust systems can remove moist air in processes that generate moisture. OSHA expects employers will typically use commercially available dehumidifiers where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fans as an engineering control: benefits and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Fans circulate air and can increase evaporative and convective heat loss, are inexpensive and portable, and are used in many workplaces (ceiling fans, pedestal fans, chair fans, ducted systems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies show fans can lower occupational heat strain at lower cost than AC; fans allow local/personalized cooling. However, fans may interfere with ventilation for airborne contaminants and could increase exposures; in some high-temperature conditions fan use alone can increase heat-strain hazard. Employers should evaluate contamination interactions and thermal conditions when using fans. OSHA requests information on settings where fans are not feasible or contraindicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identification of areas where fan use may be harmful (AT > 102 °F)
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed rule requires employers utilizing fans in indoor work areas or break areas to identify any such areas where the ambient temperature (AT) exceeds 102 °F in order to evaluate whether fan use may be harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes research showing fan use under certain high-temperature conditions can increase hazard; the agency seeks comments on indoor settings experiencing temperatures above 102 °F and on what controls employers implement when fan use is contraindicated or temperatures exceed 102 °F.

rubrics_metrics.name: WBGT instrument accuracy, equilibration, calibration, and operator training
rubrics_metrics.description: Some WBGT monitors (particularly lower-cost, non-standard devices) may not accurately measure employee heat exposure due to inconsistent equilibration times, non-robust calibration procedures, and non-standard sensor designs (smaller globes, relative-humidity-based wet-bulb calculations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical considerations affect measurement sensitivity and reliability. OSHA anticipates improvements since earlier reviews but emphasizes that proper calibration procedures and operator training are needed to ensure accurate WBGT measurements; the extent of training varies by monitor type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary conclusion: monitoring & control technologies broadly commercially available
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA preliminarily concludes that the technologies necessary to comply with the proposed monitoring and engineering-control requirements (HI, WBGT, AT instruments; AC; fans; dehumidifiers; LEV; shielding; insulation; heat-recovery systems) exist and are commercially available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA's preliminary finding is that achieving compliance is technologically feasible for most operations most of the time; the agency seeks additional comments/data on feasibility in specific settings, equipment practicability, and situations where controls may not be feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek stakeholder data & comments on feasibility and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Throughout the technological feasibility discussion OSHA repeatedly requests comments and information on the feasibility, practicality, and challenges of measuring metrics (HI, WBGT) and implementing controls (fans, AC, shielding, isolation) in different environments and for heat-generating processes, especially outdoors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA uses stakeholder input to refine understanding of practical constraints (e.g., contamination concerns with fans, calibration/training burdens, situations where AC is impractical) and to identify settings where the proposed requirements may pose challenges or require alternative approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporative coolers as an engineering control
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaporative coolers operate by passing air over a pad or surface saturated with water to produce cooling (used as an identified engineering control).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They are mentioned as an option where appropriate; suitability depends on ambient humidity and worksite conditions. (The document begins discussion of evaporative coolers but additional specifics appear later in the NPRM.)
